INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

In this action, P.B. and J.B., the parents of
the defendant R.V.E., sue her for defamation in connection with oral and
written communications to certain of her siblings in September 2003 and March
2004, and communications to all of her siblings and their spouses in October
2004.  It is pleaded that these communications contain statements that the
plaintiff P.B. sexually and physically abused the defendant, and that the
plaintiff J.B. was aware of sexual and physical abuse by the plaintiff P.B.,
and knowingly allowed it to occur and to continue.

[
2
]

The defendant, R.V.E., says that the
communications are protected by qualified privilege.  She also pleads truth.
She counterclaims against her father P.B. for damages for sexual assault and
physical assault and against her mother J.B. for breach of a fiduciary duty and
breach of a duty of care in failing to take steps to protect her from these
alleged assaults, which she pleads the plaintiff J.B. knew or ought to have
known were continuing.

[
3
]

At the end of the trial, the plaintiffs sought
to amend the statement of claim to plead publication of the defamation to
certain uncles of the defendant and friends of the plaintiffs.  I reserved on
that application.

[
4
]

I heard testimony from numerous witnesses,
mostly from the extended B. family.

[
5
]

I find that it will be appropriate to deal with
the counterclaim first and then discuss the allegations of defamation.

BACKGROUND

[
6
]

First let me set out the relevant facts and
outline some of the areas of dispute.

[
7
]

The plaintiff, J.B., was born in 1935 in Kirvoy,
Ukraine.  After the Second World War in 1945, she ended up in Germany, where
she completed grade 8.

[
8
]

On July 29, 1954, she gave birth to a daughter,
R. (now the defendant R.V.E.), who was born out of wedlock.

[
9
]

In 1955, J.B. moved to Canada with her then
almost one-year-old daughter.  She settled in Regina where two of her aunts and
uncles were living.

[
10
]

The plaintiff, P.B., was born on July 4, 1934 in
Yugoslavia.  He became a refugee at sixteen and went to Italy.  He left Italy
in 1953 and went to France for approximately one year.  In 1954, as a 20 year
old man, he moved to Canada as a refugee.  He initially worked at a power plant
for the City of Regina.

[
11
]

J.B. worked as a cleaner at the hospital and
also found employment in a restaurant, where she met P.B..  They married on
December 26, 1956 after a nine-month courtship.

[
12
]

Soon after his marriage to J.B., P.B. formally
adopted R.V.E.  P.B. and J.B. did not tell R.V.E. that she was adopted, a fact
she did not learn until she was in her early twenties.

[
13
]

After a work-related injury, P.B. began working
as a painter, which he did for over eleven years.  Initially, he worked for
another company, but from about 1964, he worked for himself.  J.B. generally
worked at home.

[
14
]

R.V.E. is one of five children.  Her sister A.K.
is four years younger (born on April 28, 1958).  She also has three younger
brothers: P.B. Jr. (born on May 30, 1959); T.B. (born on December 12, 1960);
and, E.B. (born on June 22, 1963).

[
15
]

The family lived in Regina on Lindsay Street
until 1960, then moved to Pasqua Street where they lived for just over ten
years. In 1971, the family moved to Burnaby, British Columbia.

[
16
]

By 1964, R.V.E. was ten years old.  She testified
that in the years between 1964 and 1968, she was sexually abused by P.B..
These allegations are denied by P.B.

[
17
]

Her allegations against him are as follows:

(a)       being
groped around her breasts while in a car driving back from Esterhazy,
Saskatchewan;

(b)       having
her genitals and breasts fondled:

i.          at
P.B.’s office in Regina

ii.         in
the family’s trailer

iii.        on
a number of occasions under the covers in her bed

iv.        in
her home while discussing the purchase of a bathing suit

(c)        being
grabbed and groped while playing in a lake at Fort Qu’Appelle, Saskatchewan.

[
18
]

The defendant R.V.E. testified that she could
not recall exactly when the incidents started, although she believed the first
occasion was on a trip with her father to Esterhazy.  She could not recall how
many incidents there were, as the fondling under her bed covers, she testified,
occurred repeatedly and over a period of time.

[
19
]

The defendant testified that she spoke to her
mother J.B. around 1967 about the fact that her father was “doing things to her”
and testified that she pleaded to her mother that she not leave her alone in
the house with him.  She testified that her mother asked her if he had asked
her to touch him.  J.B. denies this conversation.  R.V.E. says that the abuse
continued after this discussion.

[
20
]

According to the defendant, the sexual abuse
stopped in 1968 after the incident at Fort Qu’Appelle.  However, she testified
that P.B.’s physical abuse and name-calling continued until she left home to be
married at age 20.

[
21
]

The B. siblings always had a close
relationship.  To outsiders, the relationship of R.V.E. and her mother and
father was at least respectful.  The plaintiffs testified that their family was
a happy and close one.  R.V.E. testified that under that veneer there was, for
a period of time, sexual abuse, and for a longer period, physical and verbal
abuse.

[
22
]

The plaintiffs, in addition to denying that
there was any sexual abuse, deny that there was any physical abuse or
name-calling.

[
23
]

R.V.E. testified that although the sexual
assaults by her father stopped by around 1968, she became hyper-vigilant.  She
described her father, in Regina, becoming obsessed with following her, and that
he was often waiting in his car at her school at lunch.  This stalking, she
said, accelerated in grade 10 and 11.

[
24
]

The family moved to Burnaby when she was 17 and
she went to grade 12.  Although her father did not continue to follow her to
school, she described ongoing obsessive behaviour on his part concerning her
possible communications with boys.

[
25
]

After high school, R.V.E. worked at a bank and
then left home to go to nursing school.  She did not apply herself, she said.
She withdrew from nursing school and then went to community college.

[
26
]

She met her future husband, F.V.E.  They were
married on December 28, 1974, within seven months of meeting.

[
27
]

Prior to her wedding, R.V.E. was raped by a man
at work.  She agreed on cross-examination this was her first experience with
sexual intercourse and it was a serious and traumatic event, but she said that
she got through it.

[
28
]

Each of the plaintiffs’ children married and it
appears that the extended B. family got together relatively frequently.

[
29
]

In 1976, when R.V.E. was 22, on a visit to show
her grandmother her new baby, an important event occurred.  An aunt told R.V.E.
that P.B. was not her natural father.  She described this revelation as
humiliating, but also as a relief.  Molesting, she testified, “was better than
incest”.  She said that she felt excruciating pain for her mother “sacrificing
her to that man”.  She said that she returned to Vancouver and was met by P.B.
at the airport, who said that nothing had changed.  According to R.V.E., P.B.
told her that her mother J.B. asked her not to talk about it.

[
30
]

In 2003, an event occurred that R.V.E. says gave
rise to the circumstances that have resulted in this litigation.

[
31
]

R.V.E. and her husband have two daughters, who
are now both married.  At some point in 2003, R.V.E.’s daughter, A.H., took her
two children to visit her grandparents, P.B and J.B.  After lunch, A.H. looked
for her five-year-old daughter, M.H., who had apparently wandered off in the
house and found her in a bed with, or in a bed next to, her grandfather.  P.B.
has a condition that results in low blood sugar.  He testified that he went off
for a nap, fell asleep and never knew that M.H. had come into the room.

[
32
]

There is a dispute in the evidence as to which
room P.B. was in and whether he and his granddaughter were in the same bed.
Both R.V.E. and her daughter A.H. questioned M.H. and ultimately determined
that nothing untoward had occurred.  It was not suggested during this trial
that M.H. was molested by her grandfather, P.B.

[
33
]

A.H., however, was concerned about the incident
and telephoned her mother R.V.E. when she got home.  R.V.E. testified that she
was upset, but told her daughter not to mention it to her other daughter, M.B.,
as she was shortly to be married.  That wedding took place on June 7, 2003.
There is a dispute in the evidence whether this event with M.H. occurred before
or after the wedding.  The plaintiffs suggest that the so-called M.H. incident
occurred after M.B.’s wedding and challenge that it has the significance that
the defendant attaches to it.

[
34
]

Subsequently, the defendant sent a series of
letters and emails, first to her parents, then to her sister A.K., and then to
her siblings and their spouses.

[
35
]

The plaintiffs plead that R.V.E. sent a
defamatory email on March 18, 2004 and defamatory letters in September 2003 and
October, 2004.  The letters included a ten-page letter that is undated and
addressed to R.V.E.’s siblings and their spouses.  The plaintiffs allege the
letter is defamatory in that it contains false allegations that P.B. physically
and sexually abused R.V.E. and called her objectionable names.  According to
the pleadings of plaintiffs, they also allege it is defamatory in that it
states J.B. was aware of the physical and sexual abuse and knowingly allowed it
to occur and continue.  The plaintiffs also plead that the defendant published
false allegations of abuse of M.H.

[
36
]

The plaintiffs assert that notwithstanding their
demand, R.V.E. refused to apologize for her “defamatory and scandalous
conduct”.  The plaintiffs then started this action for damages for defamation.
The defendant pleaded that in May 2003, her daughter, A.H., found her
granddaughter, M.H., in bed and under the covers with P.B. and that the
plaintiffs have communicated to other members of the parties’ family that they
did not know why the defendant R.V.E. was upset with them and that she was
“crazy”.  The defendant says that the words alleged to be published (the
relevant paragraphs of the Amended Statement of Claim are attached as Appendix
A to this judgment) were true in substance and fact.  She claimed that they
were, in any event, published on privileged occasions and without malice.
R.V.E. has counterclaimed for damages for sexual and physical abuse.

[
37
]

Both sides to this litigation have testified
about the impact on their lives of the events that give rise to their claims
and this litigation.

[
38
]

P.B. and J.B. described the serious impact of
the alleged defamation on their family and how it has torn it apart.

[
39
]

At this point, I will set out some of R.V.E.’s
evidence of the impact that the alleged physical and sexual abuse has had on
her through her adult years.

[
40
]

R.V.E. described problems of anxiety and
depression, alcoholism, chronic pain, and difficulty sleeping.

[
41
]

R.V.E. said she was eager and happy to get
married in 1974, but she found any intimate touching took her back to being
molested.  She described disclosing to her husband several years into their
marriage, after they were watching a movie about incest, what had occurred with
her father.  I will discuss later whether that evidence is admissible and, if
so, for what purpose.

[
42
]

She testified that she needs sleeping pills even
to sleep a few hours.  She first took them when she was pregnant with her first
child and now says she cannot sleep without sleeping pills, waking within an
hour or two with a start and her heart pounding.  The nightmares that interrupt
her sleep, since 2003, have been about family conflict.

[
43
]

She described a long-standing problem with
alcohol, which started when she was a newlywed.  Drinking, she said, initially
had a positive effect.  She could loosen up and dance and enjoy sex, but it
became a concern.  She described a black depression while living in the
apartment in Burnaby, where she drank by herself.  Her drinking increased to a
litre of wine a day and it strained her relationship with her husband.  In
1992, she joined Alcoholics Anonymous.  Dr. Hedges, an addiction doctor,
put her on antidepressants and medication to prevent seizures from withdrawal.

[
44
]

She described herself as easily startled and
testified she never takes showers because she feels too vulnerable.  She
developed a fear of flying and going across bridges.

[
45
]

R.V.E. had a serious car accident in 1994, where
she broke some ribs and her sternum.  Although those injuries healed, she
continued to suffer aches and chronic pain.  She was also injured in a later
car accident.

[
46
]

Much of her chronic pain she attributed to
rheumatoid arthritis, but she has overall muscle pain as well for which she
takes Prednisone.

[
47
]

She said that she has a loud ringing in her ears
all the time, which she attributes to physical abuse from her father, P.B.

[
48
]

R.V.E. had a malignant melanoma removed from her
shoulder,

but her cancer is presently in remission.

[
49
]

Since being sued by her parents, she testified
that she first felt a sadness, then an “anger at the injustice”.  She said it
has ruined her life and that of her husband.

[
50
]

Since February 1979, she has worked as a lab
assistant at B.C. Biomedical, having worked there for twenty-six years, but is
presently on long-term disability.

[
51
]

She described trying to get back to work and not
being able to.  It appears that she stopped working after her daughter M.B.’s
wedding.  Her impediment in getting back to work, she described, is
excruciating pain, lack of sleep, and the ringing in her ears.  She testified
that she does not believe she will ever return to work.

ISSUES

[
52
]

The issues in this trial, in general terms, are:

(a)       Did the defendant defame the plaintiffs, or either of
them, and if so, are her communications subject to qualified privilege?

(b)       Is the plaintiff P.B. liable for damages for physical and
sexual assault?

(c)        Is
the plaintiff J.B. liable for damages for breach of fiduciary duty or breach of
a duty of care?

[
53
]

Because truth is raised as a defence to the
allegations of defamation, I have decided that the most logical way to consider
all of the issues in this case is to first discuss the allegations of sexual
and physical assault.

[
54
]

I will discuss the claims of R.V.E. and then
discuss the claims of defamation made by the plaintiffs.

DEFENDANT’S
ALLEGATIONS OF SEXUAL AND PHYSICAL ABUSE AND NAME-CALLING

[
55
]

The sexual abuse is alleged to have occurred
roughly in the four years prior to R.V.E. beginning high school.  The physical
abuse is alleged to have occurred up to the time the defendant left home.  It
is alleged by the defendant that the physical abuse occurred much longer than
the sexual abuse did, and accelerated when the sexual abuse stopped.

[
56
]

The allegations of sexual abuse (and physical
abuse) and name-calling are denied by the plaintiff, P.B., who suggests that
there are other reasons why the defendant is making these assertions that have
led to his claim in defamation.  These, his counsel argues, include jealousy,
upset over being P.B.’s adopted child, upset over a lack of inheritance
obtained from her natural father, and an attempt to obtain an inheritance or
money from her parents before the rest of her siblings.

[
57
]

First, I will review the parties’ evidence
generally and set out the particular allegations of R.V.E. and her parents’
response.

R.V.E.’s
Allegations at Trial

[
58
]

According to R.V.E., the first inappropriate
sexual contact occurred when she accompanied her father on a day trip to
Esterhazy, Saskatchewan.  She said she had been typing his letters, bids, bills
and tenders for his painting business for about three years.  He went to
Esterhazy to collect an account and asked if she wanted to come along and see
what she had been typing about.  She said she did.  She testified that the trip
there was uneventful, but on the way home he asked her if she wanted an ice
cream cone (something she said was not typical).  As they drove home, he asked
her if she wished to drive by putting a hand on the wheel.  She said she
“scooted over” towards him on the bench seat, and that the next thing she knew
he put his arm around her and touched her breast.  She testified that she was
quite shocked, but was not sure why.  She testified that it was “yucky” and
felt “bad, but different from a beating”.  She did not talk to anyone about it
at the time.

[
59
]

The second incident, or the one she said that
she thought was the second incident, occurred in an office he obtained for his
business in 1967.  Even when he had an office she testified that P.B. would
bring stationery home for her to do some typing.  One night he said to her
“let’s do this letter at the office”.  She said that they went to the office,
which she had not seen before, and sat at the desk.  Instead of having notes
that she read from, she said that he lifted her up and put her on his lap.  She
testified that he put his hands down her pants and her underpants and started
groping her.  She testified that she was horrified and he pulled his hand out.
She asked “what are you doing – does mom know what you are doing”.  She
testified that he said that: “mom can’t know” and “she would be so mad and our
family would be blown apart”.  She said she asked him “why are you doing this
if it is a bad thing?” and he said that “it is because I love you and I can not
help it that I love you”.  She said that made her feel sicker and then they
went home.  She said that she felt disgusted and “wanted to pour boiling water”
over herself.  She testified that she felt there must be something really wrong
with her.

[
60
]

R.V.E. then described the next incident, but she
said she was not sure if it was the third or the fifth incident.  She said that
there were times during the summer holidays when her parents were away from
home that she had to stay at home, watch the business phone, and pick it up
after three rings.  She testified that after 1968 her mother worked at Sears,
and sometimes she liked to get out of the house and make a day of it.  She said
she would watch the phones while her siblings were outside playing with their
bikes.  She said that as her father had his own business, he would “pop in” and
visit the grandmothers or “pop in at home”, any time.  R.V.E. said his
molesting had not happened at home and she did not expect it to happen there.

[
61
]

One day, her father came into the house in a
good mood.  She said that she had to get his permission (to buy a bathing suit)
and she showed him a catalogue.  She said that he said that “the one that you
have is so much nicer” and she said that he ran his hands over “every bathing
suit area”, which I understood to be a reference to the private areas of her
body.  She said she ran outside.  She testified that it was sometime after this
that she told her mother that P.B. was doing “bad things” to her.

[
62
]

R.V.E. testified that she spent the days looking
out the windows to see if P.B. was coming.  She described being terrified and
panicking.  R.V.E. said that this was the reason she told her mother, J.B..
R.V.E. says she told her mother “don’t leave me in the house; he does bad
things to me” and her mother’s response was only a question: “did he ask you to
touch him”.  The defendant said no and that her mother, she said, was
dismissive and said that it was “always something”.  The defendant said she was
11 or 12 years old at this time, gauging where she was at school.

[
63
]

After the alleged conversation with her mother,
she said there was no change in her father’s behaviour and she was sexually
assaulted by him.

[
64
]

R.V.E. described an episode that occurred in a
trailer that, she said, was parked in her paternal grandmother’s driveway.  She
testified that the family was going to take it out for a weekend and she and
her sister were there to clean it up.  P.B., she testified, showed up at her
grandmother’s and sent her sister A.K. from the trailer into the house to get
something.  R.V.E. testified, “no sooner was she gone than (he) was on the bed,
he pulled me down” and she said he groped her.  She said he put his hands in
her pants and underwear, and on her genitals.  She described his hands as
“rough rotten painter hands”.  He poked her in her genitals with his fingers.
She said his other arm was around her holding on to her chest and that he was
“rapid talking”.  She said it continued for minutes until her sister got back.
She said that they then carried on like nothing happened.  She said she did not
tell anyone else as she had already gone to her mother and she felt there was
nowhere else to go.

[
65
]

After that, R.V.E. said that P.B. periodically
came into a bedroom she shared with her sister, when they were in bed.  She
testified that he would sit on her sister’s bed, talk to her sister and reach
back and stick his hands in her pyjama pants.  She said she would try to squirm
to the other side of the bed, but said there was not far to go.  She described
that this went on for minutes.  She testified that she was dead quiet during it
and said nothing.  She described this as happening maybe “fifteen times or
under” in the later grades of elementary school.  She said that she felt
hopeless and depressed, before she knew what that term meant.  She said she
felt cornered and trapped.  She testified that she was stymied by the lack of
reaction by her mother and was too afraid and ashamed to tell other relatives.

[
66
]

When asked if there were other incidents, she
testified that when she was in grade 7 or 8, her family went to the lake at
Fort Qu’Appelle.  Her siblings were in the lake and her parents stayed on the
shore.  Motorboats made waves, and the children would play in them.  She said
that her father was in the water and put a hand on her waist and his hand on
her crotch and said “see how nice and tight it fits here, it fits nice”.  She
said her mother J.B. was on the shore and yelled at P.B.  She said her father
went to her mother and said “it’s not what you think, we were just playing”.
She said she stood in the lake dumbfounded and helpless.  She testified that
her mother said nothing to her about this.

[
67
]

R.V.E. testified that she believed the incident
at Fort Qu’Appelle was the last time she was sexually abused.  She said she
became hyper-vigilant.  In high school, she said, her father became obsessed
about where she went and followed her.

[
68
]

In terms of physical discipline and
name-calling, the defendant said that her father hit her “as far back as she
could remember”.

[
69
]

She said that her mother did not hit her as
much; she said it was occasionally a smack sometimes on the face or with a tea
towel, something she described as happening less than five times a year.  She
described her mother’s hitting as a momentary reaction.  She said her mother
periodically hit the children, but never her sister A.K., rarely her brother
E.B., but gave her brother P.B. Jr. some “good lickings” and hit her brother
T.B. periodically.

[
70
]

R.V.E. said that her father hit her with his
hands, both open and closed.  She said that he hit her frequently on the face
or wherever his hands landed.  She testified she was always sore, and indicated
the nose pad where her glasses rested.  She said he “just went off, you never
knew”.  She testified that while he was hitting her he would call her names,
depending on her age, things like: “you’re nothing but a rat” or “an animal” or
“you’re a punk”, “you’re a pig”.

[
71
]

She said she would shield herself, and be hit on
the back or her shoulders, or the side of the head. She said when he flew into
a real rage, he pummelled her.  She said he often pulled her hair and banged her
head against the wall.

[
72
]

She testified that she was hard-pressed to come
up with a number of times that he struck her with a belt.  He would grab hold
of her hand or wrist and whip away.  She said she got it on the back of her
legs and arms and got hit with the buckle side; when he hit her with the belt,
she said it was more than once.

[
73
]

She said that he hit her on the side of her
head, he hit her glasses and they broke.  She testified that her glasses broke
over and over again; they were taped or melted and finally the arm had to be
replaced.  She said that they were fixed by her father, a smoker at the time,
who melted the arm and put it together.  Her glasses were broken a couple of
dozen times and it became, she said, a standing joke in the family.

[
74
]

She testified that P.B. hit the other children,
except A.K.  She said that he beat P.B. Jr. numerous times.  She said he hit
T.B., beat him, but far less times but the severity, she said, was there.  She
said he hit P.B. Jr. and T.B. both with closed and open hands and with a belt.
She testified that she could not really recall whether he hit E.B.

[
75
]

She also described a form of discipline her
father regularly imposed where the children had to kneel in the corner until
they said that they were sorry.  She also said they were occasionally
disciplined with popcorn (having to kneel on it).  The popcorn punishment
occurred about twice a year, she said, but it was only P.B. Jr. and her that
received that form of punishment.  She testified that this kind of punishment
did not occur on the occasion that her parents described in their testimony.

[
76
]

She described an occasion when her glasses
slipped into the dishwater.  She said her father said, “you are always trying
to get attention you little bitch”, and he hit her.  She described another

General
Principles Concerning Credibility and the Standard of Proof

[
122
]

I will first consider the standard of proof where there are
allegations of sexual, physical and verbal abuse.

[
123
]

The defendant’s allegations in this case are very serious.

[
124
]

When there are serious claims, such as sexual or physical abuse, the
court has taken an approach commensurate with the gravity of the allegations.  In
such cases, the court must take greater care in scrutinizing the evidence when
an allegation of serious misconduct is being made.

[
125
]

As the Court of Appeal recently noted in
C.(R.). v. McDougall
,

2007 BCCA 212
, 68 B.C.L.R. (4th) 203, where the allegations involve morally
blameworthy conduct, there is a more stringent standard of proof to be applied
in a civil suit for sexual abuse.  Rowles, J.A. said:

[30]      The common law recognizes that in
cases where morally blameworthy conduct is alleged, the evidence must be
scrutinized with care and the civil standard of proof applied so that it is
"commensurate with the occasion":
Bater v. Bater
,

[1950] 2 All E.R. 458 at 459 (Eng. C.A.)
.

[31]      In
Continental Insurance Co. v.
Dalton Cartage Co.
,
1982 CanLII 13 (SCC)
, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 164 (S.C.C.) at 169-171, Laskin
C.J., for the Court, stated:

Where there is an allegation of conduct
that is morally blameworthy or that could have a criminal or penal aspect and
the allegation is made in civil litigation, the relevant burden of proof
remains proof on a balance of probabilities. …

… There is necessarily a matter of
judgment involved in weighing evidence that goes to the burden of proof, and a
trial judge is justified in scrutinizing evidence with greater care if there
are serious allegations to be established by the proof that is offered. …

I do not regard such an approach as a
departure from a standard of proof based on a balance of probabilities nor as
supporting a shifting standard.  The question in all civil cases is what
evidence with what weight that is accorded to it will move the court to
conclude that proof on a balance of probabilities has been established.

[
126
]

At ¶78-79, Rowles J.A. discussed the need to apply the civil
standard in a way that is “commensurate with the occasion.” In doing so, she
found the trial judge had erred in law for failing to consider serious
inconsistencies in the plaintiff's evidence in determining whether the fact of
sexual assault had been proved to the standard commensurate with the allegation:

[78]      When the respondent's case concerning
the sexual assaults turned entirely on his testimony, the trial judge was bound
to scrutinize and weigh his evidence with great care….

[79]      It
appears to me that at the very least, when the respondent's testimony stood
alone, the trial judge was bound to consider , among other things, the serious
inconsistencies in the respondent’s evidence in determining whether the fact in
issue had been proved to the standard commensurate with the allegation.  In my
respectful view, the trial judge did not scrutinize the evidence in the manner
required and thereby erred in law.

[
127
]

As such, in civil cases involving serious claims of sexual and
physical assault, the appropriate standard to apply is one based on the balance
of probabilities with careful scrutiny of the evidence
in a manner that is proportionate with the serious claims being alleged.

[
128
]

I also think that it is important to have in mind these oft-repeated
comments on assessing credibility that appeared more than fifty years ago in
Faryna
v. Chorny
(1951),
1951 CanLII 252 (BC CA)
, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354 (B.C.C.A.), at 357:

The credibility of
interested witnesses, particularly in cases of conflict of evidence, cannot be
gauged solely by the test of whether the personal demeanour of the particular
witness carried conviction of the truth.  The test must reasonably subject his
story to an examination of its consistency with the probabilities that surround
the currently existing conditions.  In short, the real test of the truth of the
story of a witness in such a case must be its harmony with the preponderance of
the probabilities which a practical and informed person would readily recognize
as reasonable in that place and in those conditions.  Only thus can a court satisfactorily
appraise the testimony of quick-minded, experienced and confident witnesses,
and of those shrewd persons adept in the half-lie and of long and successful
experience in combining skilful exaggeration with partial suppression of the
truth.  Again a witness may testify what he sincerely believes to be true, but
he may be quite honestly mistaken.  For a trial judge to say "I believe
him because I judge him to be telling the truth," is to come to a
conclusion on consideration of only half the problem.  In truth it may easily
be self-direction of a dangerous kind.

129
]

Although corroboration is not necessary, great care must be taken

Popplewell
,
[1994] B.C.J. No. 884 (S.C.)(Q.L.)
;

T.(W.O.),
2000 BCSC 309
, [2000] B.C.J. No. 342 (Q.L.);
Blackwater
v. Plint
,
2001 BCSC 997
,
93 B.C.L.R. (3d) 228.

The plaintiffs’ counsel suggests that there are other reasons for

[
182
]

Are the suggestions on cross-examination that
her allegations of sexual abuse and physical abuse are false, suggestions of
recent fabrications or recent concoctions?  If so, is the evidence that the
defendant sought to introduce of earlier reports to her husband and to her
doctor of sexual and physical abuse admissible to rebut the allegations of
recent fabrication?

[
183
]

Prior consistent statements are generally not
admissible.  Cory J. in
R. v.
Evans
,

1993 CanLII 102 (SCC)
, [1993] 2
S.C.R. 629
at 643,
said:

Ordinarily, other persons may not be called to testify as to a witness's
out of court statements. Nor may a witness repeat, in court, her own earlier
statements. Generally, the narration by a witness of her previous declarations
made to others outside of the court should be excluded because of its general
lack of probative value and because such a repetition is, as a rule,
self-serving. However, they may be admitted in support of the credibility of a
witness in situations where that witness's evidence is challenged as being a
recent fabrication or contrivance.

[
184
]

As to what is a recent fabrication, Finlayson J.A. provided a brief
definition in
R v. O’Connor
(1995)
,
1995 CanLII 255 (ON CA)
, 100 C.C.C. (3d)
285; 25 O.R. (3d) 19 at ¶15 (Ont. C.A.):

[15]      … an
allegation of recent fabrication is no more than an allegation that the
complainant has made up a false story to meet the exigencies of the case. The
word "recent" means that the complainant's evidence has been invented
or fabricated after the events in question and thus is a "recent"
invention or fabrication

[
185
]

I find that the suggestions in Mr. Pyper’s cross-examination of
making complaints of sexual and physical abuse to get an early advance on her
inheritance, because she and her children were not treated as generously by
J.B. as her siblings, because she did not get an inheritance from her natural
father, or because she is upset over not learning earlier that she was adopted,
are suggestions that her allegations are recently concocted.

[
186
]

In order to rebut the suggestion of recent concoction, the defendant
introduced evidence of her complaint to Dr. Hedges, an addiction specialist
that she saw in February 1993.  Dr. Hedges notes in 1993 in response to a

What was it like at home?

Awful

→ beating – dad was bully++

→ verbal/physical abuse

→ sex abuse – dad (10-14) – unable to
tell anyone

→ like the Waltons on the outside we
pretend

F.V.E. also testified that shortly after their marriage, his wife
told him about yelling and name-calling, words like bitch, slut, whore and

He said that they were watching a television program on incest and that
precipitated her telling him.  She told him that her father P.B. had sexually abused

[

]

F.V.E.’s evidence, like Dr. Hedge’s evidence, is admissible for the

[
189

In
R v. Stirling,
2007 BCCA 4
, 215 C.C.C. (3d) 208,
the Court of Appeal dealt with the issue of suggested recent fabrications and
the use of prior consistent statements.  At ¶48, Chiasson J.A. considered
R.
v. Aksidan
,
2006 BCCA 258
, [2006] B.C.W.L.D. 4412
,
a case concerning the sexual
assault of an eleven-year old girl and a videotaped statement, which was dealt
with as a prior consistent statement.  In
Aksidan
,
the court said
at ¶21:

[21]      … the
prior consistent statement is relevant only to the credibility or reliability
of the in-court testimony of the witness.  It may be used to rebut the
allegation of recent fabrication and thus rehabilitate the witness's
credibility but it may not be used for its truth or as confirmatory of the
in-court testimony of the witness, since it is hearsay for those purposes: see
R.
v. W.(G.)
(1998),
1998 CanLII 18052 (NL CA)
, 18 C.R. (5th) 379 paragraph
43
(Nfld. C.A.); Sopinka,
Lederman, and Bryant,
The Law of Evidence in Canada
, 2d ed. (Toronto and
Vancouver: Butterworths, 1999), p. 319, s. 7.16.

[
190
]

Based on the authorities considered in
Stirling

at ¶56,

Chiasson J.A. concluded that prior consistent statements do not add to
or strengthen the weight of the evidence of a witness.  Prior consistent
statements like the disclosures to Dr. Hedges or F.V.E. can only be used
to rebut allegations of recent fabrication.

[56]      Prior
consistent statements cannot add to or strengthen the weight of the evidence of
a witness.  They do not independently confirm that evidence, but they are
confirmatory in the sense that the in-court testimony is not a recent
fabrication, that is, the suggestion of recent fabrication having been
rebutted, the in-court testimony stands for whatever it is worth.  This conclusion
is consonant with the observations of Mr. Justice Smith and with the previous
authorities to which I have referred (
Fox v. General Medical Council
;

McWilliams' Canadian Criminal Evidence
;
The Law of Evidence in Canada
).

]

Moreover, I do not find, from a consideration of all of the

]

]

[
204
]

P.B. testified that he later visited M.H. for her birthday (A.H.
said that they were not invited) and that M.H. held his hand and asked him to

205
]

He said that A.H. is making up the accusations that he was in the
same bed with M.H. in the spare bedroom in a single bed.  He testified that he

206
]

207
]

I found A.H. to be a credible witness.  I find that P.B. was in the
same bed as M.H. and that it alarmed her mother, A.H.  I find she immediately

coherent manner.  I find that she had no reason to fabricate what occurred and
her evidence appeared very genuine and was not successfully challenged on
cross-examination.  Considering all of the evidence, I find that this incident
took place before M.B.’s wedding.

[
208
]

I do not accept P.B.’s evidence that he was asleep or in a different
bed when A.H. found him in the bed in the spare bedroom with M.H.  While

found it significant and reported it to her mother.  I found her description of
the incident, how M.H. was found, in what bedroom she was found, where her
grandfather was, and whether he was awake much more credible than the evidence
of the plaintiffs and I accept it.

[
209
]

Upon a consideration of all of the evidence, I find that there was
obvious tension involving P.B. and J.B. at M.B.’s wedding.  I find that this

written and oral communications that resulted in a letter to the siblings that
is the central publication in his defamation law suit.

[
210

At M.B.’s wedding, A.H. said that she was slapped by her grandmother

Findings on Credibility

[
213
]

Upon a consideration of all of the evidence, I have concluded that
the allegations of R.V.E. of sexual abuse, physical abuse and name-calling
against P.B. are proven.

[
214
]

I accept the evidence of R.V.E. and reject the evidence of P.B.  I
also prefer the evidence of R.V.E. to that of J.B.

[
215
]

However, as I will explain later, I do not find that the evidence of
J.B.’s knowledge of P.B.’s tortious acts and her alleged failure to act meets
the standard of proof required for liability on her part.

[
216
]

I found that the evidence of R.V.E. was credible, had the ring of
truth, and contained a sufficient level of detail that made it appear
credible.  She acknowledged that there were certain things that she could not
recall.  It was suggested in her evidence that she denied she suffers memory
loss, which was contradicted by her evidence that she had trouble remembering
under stress.  However, I did not find that to be a serious contradiction.  She
was not shown to be untruthful on cross-examination.

[
217
]

Occasionally she was opinionated about the veracity of other
people’s evidence.  She said that her father was “a liar and not a very good
one either” and described her sister’s evidence of being at the office with her
as “a fabrication”.  Those strong opinions did not negatively impact on my
assessment of her evidence.

[
218
]

Overall, R.V.E. gave her evidence in a straightforward and clear and
cogent fashion, sometimes abrupt but never, in my assessment, apparently tailored
or contrived to make it more believable.  An untruthful witness might have
purported to recall things that assisted her case, but she did not.  Often, as
I heard her evidence, I noted that her evidence had the ring of truth and was
not tailored to fit in with other evidence.  Her explanation for why her
allegations of abuse were made at the time they were was logical.  It appeared
plausible and logical that the root of her disclosures to the family started
with the M.H. incident.

[
219
]

Near the end of her cross-examination, she said she loved her
mother, which the plaintiff’s counsel suggested contradicted earlier evidence,
which in fact it did.  However, that earlier evidence, I think, was an
emotional response to her mother’s evidence.  Rather than hurting her
credibility, this apparent contradiction I found, in fact, enhanced her
credibility.  It demonstrated how difficult and conflicting these issues are
for the members of this family.  The defendant still has strong feelings of
love for her mother and rather than tailoring her evidence, expressed different
views at different times.

[

]

The plaintiff’s counsel describes R.V.E. as “a desperate, imperious
callous witness who … gave condescending and sardonic remarks about the

about the plaintiffs.  I did not see that as a badge of dishonesty, but rather
an aspect of how conflicted and upset she is by the events that have resulted
in this litigation.

[
221
]

I found R.V.E.’s explanation for why she revealed the alleged abuse
when she did and why it was brought out over time in her correspondence to be
credible and logical.

[
222
]

Overall, I found R.V.E. to be a credible and believable witness.

[
223
]

On the other hand, I found that the evidence of the plaintiffs,
particularly P.B., was not credible on the main points.

[

]

There were a number of incidents described in the evidence, and
where there was a conflict, I preferred the evidence of R.V.E. to P.B.  In a
number of these incidents, where there was evidence from a third party that
supported R.V.E.’s evidence, I found that I accepted that evidence.

[
225
]

One issue was whether P.B. broke R.V.E.’s glasses.

]

knocking her glasses off and breaking them, E.B., the youngest child, who was a

While R.V.E. was not successfully challenged on cross-examination,

The Supreme Court of Canada has recognized the

In
M.(K.) v. M.(H.)
,

1992 CanLII 31 (SCC)
, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 6 at ¶76, LaForest J. (Gonthier, Cory and Iacobucci JJ. concurring) wrote:

[76]      … The
inherent purpose of the family relationship imposes certain obligations on a
parent to act in his child's best interests, and a presumption of fiduciary

[

A parent’s fiduciary obligation obviously includes a duty to refrain

In

,
2000
BCSC 735
at ¶113-115,137, Levine J. (as she then was)

Causation

[
265
]

In this case, there is a serious issue whether the conditions that
the defendant suffers from were caused by the plaintiff P.B.’s assault.  The
plaintiffs’ counsel says that many of her complaints cannot be attributed to
P.B. and these include arthritis, chronic pain, alcoholism, depression, chronic
fatigue, fibromyalgia, malignant melanoma, contamination phobia, insomnia and
osteoporosis.  He argues that these were caused by the motor vehicle accidents,
the time she was raped as a young adult, or various unrelated illnesses.

[
266
]

The law applicable to determining causation where there are
multi-cause injuries was described in
Resurfice Corp. v.

Hanke
,

2007 SCC 7
, [2007] 1 S.C.R. 333.  In
Resurfice,
the Supreme Court
of Canada found the lower court had erred in failing to recognize that the
basic test for causation remains the "but for" test.  Further, the
Court held the Court of Appeal erred in applying the material contribution test
in circumstances where its use was neither necessary nor justified.  Chief
Justice McLachlin said at ¶19:

[19]      The
Court of Appeal erred in suggesting that, where there is more than one
potential cause of an injury, the "material contribution" test must
be used.  To accept this conclusion is to do away with the "but for"
test altogether, given that there is more than one potential cause in virtually
all litigated cases of negligence.  If the Court of Appeal's reasons in this
regard are endorsed, the only conclusion that could be drawn is that the
default test for cause-in-fact is now the material contribution test.  This is
inconsistent with this Court's judgments in
Snell v. Farrell
,

1990 CanLII 70 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 311;
Athey v. Leonati
, at para. 14;
Walker
Estate v. York Finch General Hospital
, [2001] 1 S.C.R. 647,
2001 SCC
23
, at paras.
87-88
, and
Blackwater v. Plint
, [2005] 3 S.C.R. 3,

2005 SCC 58
, at para.
78
.

[
267
]

At ¶21-23, McLachlin, C.J.C. outlined the general principles that
have emerged from the cases listed above:

[21]      First, the basic test for determining
causation remains the "but for" test.  This applies to multi-cause
injuries. The plaintiff bears the burden of showing that "but for"
the negligent act or omission of each defendant, the injury would not have
occurred.  Having done this, contributory negligence may be apportioned, as
permitted by statute.

[22]
This fundamental rule has never
been displaced and remains the primary test for causation in negligence actions
.
As stated in
Athey v. Leonati
, at para. 14, per Major J.,
"[t]he general, but not conclusive, test for causation is the 'but for'
test, which requires the plaintiff to show that the injury would not have
occurred but for the negligence of the defendant.”  Similarly, as I noted in
Blackwater
v. Plint
, at para. 78, "[t]he rules of causation consider
generally whether 'but for' the defendant's acts, the plaintiff's damages would
have been incurred on a balance of probabilities."

[23]      The
"but for" test recognizes that compensation for negligent conduct
should only be made "where a substantial connection between the injury and
the defendant's conduct" is present.  It ensures that a defendant will not
be held liable for the plaintiff's injuries where they "may very well be
due to factors unconnected to the defendant and not the fault of anyone":

Snell v. Farrell
, at p. 327, per Sopinka J.

[emphasis added]

[
268
]

In
Hutchings v. Dow,
2007 BCCA 148
, 66 B.C.L.R. (4th)
78, the trial judge found that the depression suffered by the plaintiff was an
indivisible injury that was contributed to in a material way by the accident
that was the subject of the litigation and a subsequent assault.  Prowse J.A.
said at ¶20:

[20]      In this
case, the appellants submit that the trial judge should have applied a
"but for" test in determining causation and that his failure to do so
requires that the action be remitted to the trial court for a new trial.  While
I agree that a "but for" test was the appropriate test to apply in
these circumstances, I do not agree that the trial judge's failure to frame his
reasons in "but for" language is fatal to his conclusions.  Rather, I
am satisfied that the trial judge's reasoning and findings support his
conclusions on the basis of a "but for" analysis.  In my view, it is
implicit in his reasons that the trial judge was satisfied that "but
for" the accident the depression would not have occurred, and "but
for" the assault the depression would not have occurred.  In other words,
both the accident and the assault were necessary, but not sufficient,
conditions giving rise to Mr. Hutchings' depression.  The trial judge was not
persuaded that any of the other factors relied on by the appellants (including
personal and economic problems, and a period of drug use) played any
significant causative role in Mr. Hutchings' depression and, in my view, the
evidence supports his conclusion in that regard.  In the result, I would not
give credence to this ground of appeal.

[
269
]

The defendant must establish that but for P.B.’s abuse, she would
not have suffered the psychological disorders or injuries of which she
complains, or suffered them to the extent that she has them.

[
270
]

I will try to summarize Dr. O’Shaughnessy’s evidence in
relation to causation.

[
271
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy is a psychiatrist, well qualified in the area
of claims for damages for sexual abuse, with extensive experience in evaluating
individuals traumatized in a variety of circumstances, including historical
abuse in childhood.

[
272
]

He saw R.V.E. on three occasions in 2005 for a total of 5½ hours.
He outlined in detail in his report the history that she alleges.  He noted
that at the time of his examination, she was taking Sertraline, an
anti-depressant and was taking a high dosage.  The side effects of that medication

Dextroamphetamine to augment the depression and fatigue.  For night-time
sedation she was taking Nozinan and Zopiclone, and Prednisone for chronic
arthritic pain.  She also takes Lipitor for cholesterol problems.

[
273
]

In his report, he noted that R.V.E. reported to him that she was
molested by her father over the course of two to three years prior to the onset
of her menstrual periods and described multiple episodes of abuse characterized
primarily by genital fondling as well as rubbing her chest in addition to
digital penetration of her vagina.  He noted that she denied any violence or
threats apart from threats of family turmoil if she were to disclose the
abuse.  Dr. O’Shaughnessy said there was no evidence of any overt violence nor
was there any evidence of penile penetration or oral sexual contact.  He
reported that she described her adoptive father as an extremely controlling man
with temper outbursts who was often given to physical abuse and punishment,
especially of R.V.E., and she believed that she received more physical and
emotional abuse than her younger siblings.  He reported that despite what would
appear to be a very unhappy family situation, she had some positive aspects and
seemed to enjoy a good relationship with her younger siblings.

[
274
]

As I mentioned during the trial, I am of the view that Dr.
O’Shaughnessy made no findings on whether R.V.E. was in fact physically or
sexually abused.  That is not his role.  The weight, if any, to be given to his
opinion depends on whether the underlying assumptions, that he makes, have been
proven to be true.  As I set out above, I find that the facts upon which he
based his opinion have been proven at trial.  Dr. O’Shaughnessy’s opinion
was not successfully challenged.  I found it persuasive and I accept it.

[
275
]

In terms of his diagnosis, Dr. O’Shaughnessy said that R.V.E.
had both anxiety disorders and mood disorders.  He described an anxiety
disorder as one where the predominant features are anxiety and fearfulness, the
key distinction of a disorder from normalcy is that there is a significant
disability in social and work situations.  He said the cause of an anxiety
disorder can be genetic or can be a reaction to traumatic events.  He said that
in addition to her mood disorders, she had a significant anxiety disorder that
seems to have begun in her teens and twenties and persisted to the current
time.  He said that she met the criteria for obsessive-compulsive disorder as
well as post-traumatic stress disorder, with partial remission of both
illnesses.

[
276
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy said that she suffers from a mood disorder,
something which is either a high or low mood, in her case low.  She suffers
from depression, for which she is treated with antidepressants.  He said that
she would be described as having chronic depression with partial remission
through medication.

[
277
]

On cross-examination, Dr. O’Shaughnessy agreed that the weight his
report deserves depends on whether the facts as reported to him are correct.
He described the determination that she was adopted as an unpleasant event
rather than a traumatic event.  He was of a view that it was unlikely that the
sexual assault at age twenty caused the alcoholism.  He said that her alcohol
problem became more prevalent by age thirty.  He agreed that a single rape is a
traumatic event, and he agreed that it can cause post-traumatic stress disorder
and it is most common cause among women in North America.  He was asked
whether, assuming the sexual abuse took place as a child, you cannot
distinguish the rape and the childhood sexual abuse in the culmination of
post-traumatic stress disorder.

[
278
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy said that post-traumatic stress disorder is
an anxiety disorder triggered by frightening events, traumatic memories and
intrusive memories that cannot be suppressed.  He said you look at the
traumatic memories, the intrusive memories that cannot be suppressed.  He said
if you look at the intrusive memories of people who have multiple traumatic events
it helps you distinguish.  Dr. O’Shaughnessy said that R.V.E. reported
that the memories had more to do with the fondling than with the rape.  He said
that post-traumatic stress disorder follows frightening events such as sexual
assaults, physical assaults and car accidents.  He said that menopause would
not be a factor in post-traumatic stress disorder but would play a role in mood
disorders.  He agreed that R.V.E. has a long-standing lack of confidence and
self-worth.

[
279
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy said that the symptoms of post-traumatic stress
disorder include intrusive memories, nightmares, flashbacks of the abuse by her
father, often triggered by sexual intimacy.  He said that like many individuals
who have post-traumatic stress disorder from sexual abuse, R.V.E. also
experiences significant sexual dysfunction with initial problems related to
lack of arousal as well as anorgasmic difficulty.  In the general population,
about fifty percent of post-traumatic stress disorder clears up without
intervention, but as to the balance he hesitates to use the word “cure” because
in psychiatry problems tend to be chronic.  He said that there was a crossover
in the area of mood and anxiety disorders.

[
280
]

In terms of her obsessive-compulsive disorder, which he described as
being in partial remission, he said she was quite ritualistic with the need to
have everything neat, controlled, tidy, primarily characterized by checking
behaviours on stoves, door locks, multiple times each day.  He also said she
has some degree of generalized anxiety symptoms, although these are controlled
by the medications.

[
281
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy said that all of her disorders are in partial
remission because of medication.  If she were to discontinue the medication, he
thought that she would no doubt have a full recurrence of depression and likely
a significant increase in symptoms of anxiety.  Dr. O’Shaughnessy described
that over the last three years, as exacerbated by the family strife, her
post-traumatic stress disorder would be described as chronic, a term used in
psychiatry when the disorder lasts beyond an arbitrary period of six months.

[
282
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy noted in his report that R.V.E. did not have any
evidence of marked difficulties or behavioural problems prior to the abuse or
assaults.  Based on her description he said it is likely she was exposed to
significant emotional and physical abuse over and above the sexual abuse.

[
283
]

He opined that abuse that is non-violent and non-penetrating and
consists primarily of fondling and touching is much less severe in its
pathological effect than penetrating offences or violent offences, and he would
consider the abuse that she described as in the moderate range, given that it
was intra-familial, but not violent or penetrating.  He described the
difference between adult abuse and childhood sexual abuse is that although both
can cause post-traumatic stress disorder, in a child it occurs during a
developmental stage.  He said that one distinction between extra-familial and
intra-familial abuse is that not only is there trauma and the disruption of the
developmental aspect, but there is the interference with the normal
parent-child relationship, creating problems with trust issues.
Dr. O’Shaughnessy in his report noted that there were significant family
problems related to secrets and lack of disclosure that may well have played a
significant role in her vulnerability.  He noted that when one looks at the
combined vulnerability and trauma factors, one would conclude that she would
more likely than not develop significant psychological sequelae as a result of
this abuse (that she alleges).  He said that the psychiatric literature
indicates that people who have been sexually abused in childhood have an
increased rate of psychiatric disorder in a variety of areas.

[
284
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy discussed the relationship between the abuse
described by the defendant and her psychological problems.  I recognize that
there are certain things that R.V.E. suffers from that were not caused by the
assault, namely her arthritis, her injuries from the motor vehicle accidents
that have resulted in chronic pain, the malignant melanoma, and osteoporosis.

[
285
]

Whether, in his opinion, the defendant would have developed
post-traumatic stress disorder, the anxiety disorder and the personality
problems had she not been sexually abused by P.B., Dr. O’Shaughnessy said,
“probably not”.

[
286
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy described her alcohol abuse as starting off
mildly, but ultimately increasing and becoming a disorder.  He said she clearly
had problems in her relationship caused by alcohol.

[
287
]

In connection with her alcohol abuse, Dr. O’Shaughnessy said in his
report:

Bearing in mind
the data in this case, it would be my opinion that the sexual abuse was more
likely than not a critical factor in the subsequent development of her
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and Anxiety Disorder as well as her personality
problems.  Further, it played a significant role in the onset of her substance
abuse difficulties.  [R.V.E.] describes the onset of alcohol use in large
measure to deal with her underlying anxiety both socially as well as sexually.
Alcohol is a CNS depressant that does indeed reduce anxiety but unfortunately
carries with it is own significant morbidity.  I have little doubt that the use
of alcohol was primarily as an anxiolytic initially and later became an
addiction.  It is likely that her alcohol abuse would not have occurred had the
sexual abuse not occurred and the subsequent anxiety been caused.

[
288
]

Dr. O’Shaughnessy said this about R.V.E.’s depression in his written
report:

[R.V.E.’s] depression is more complicated in
that clearly it is also related to chronic pain difficulties.  It is difficult
to evaluate how much of her depression is directly related to childhood abuse.
Certainly childhood abuse increases the vulnerability to adult depression but
also biological factors play a significant role in the genesis of depression.
It appears she had evidence of depression before the car accident when she was
also drinking heavily.  The depression was much worse after she developed
chronic pain.  It is probable the sexual abuse played a significant role in
causing the initial depression but other factors contributed to the severity of
her Mood Disorder.

In my view,
[R.V.E.’s] sexual dysfunction is a direct relationship to the sexual abuse.
This is in fact a common outcome and she would not have developed this degree
of sexual dysfunction had the abuse not occurred.  This in turn has also been a
factor in her marital relationship although fortunately she has enjoyed a
supportive relationship with her husband.  It is likely that her relationship
has been a critical factor moderating the impact of her illness and providing a
great deal of emotional and social support for her.  Had this marriage not been
as supportive, she more likely than not would have been much more disabled.

[
289
]

In the context of the car accident, Dr. O’Shaughnessy was asked
whether she would have developed depression in the absence of sexual abuse by
her stepfather.  Dr. O’Shaughnessy said that this was a complicated issue.  He
said evidence of depression pre-dated the accident but that her injuries in it
aggravated the depression.  He said that he thought her depression was more
likely related to the post-traumatic stress disorder and sexual abuse.  He said
her depression now is increased by a variety of other factors.  He expected
that she will need antidepressant medication for the foreseeable future.

[
290
]

In his opinion in describing the complexity of this situation, he
noted that there is not a one-to-one relationship between childhood abuse and
adult psychiatric sequelae, as there are many other factors.  For example, in
her case, chronic pain, he thought, plays a significant role in her
depression.  He described it as a “chicken and egg” situation.  Here, it is
more complex, he said, because there is ample evidence that people that develop
chronic pain have a higher level of traumatic events in childhood, including
sexual abuse.

[
291
]

He said that people can show the same symptoms without being
sexually abused.  He said when you see these things in the context of sexual
abuse, the sexual abuse is more likely a material factor.  Possibly they would
occur, but on a balance of probabilities, he said, probably not.

[
292
]

I find that based on Dr. O’Shaughnessy’s opinion, which I accept,
R.V.E. has diagnosed disorders that I find were caused, at least in part by,
and would not have occurred but for, the abuse inflicted by the plaintiff,
P.B.  Those conditions are (1) major depressive disorder in partial
remission; (2) post-traumatic stress disorder in partial remission; (3) an
obsessive compulsive disorder in partial remission; (4) sexual dysfunction
in good remission; and (5) substance abuse currently in remission.

[
293
]

Although she is currently having an increase in all of her symptoms,
in large measure due to the effects of the litigation and the disruption of the
family, Dr. O’Shaughnessy thought that once the litigation had completed
her symptoms will again diminish.

[
294
]

In terms of her ability to return to work, Dr. O’Shaughnessy
stated that this was complicated as it is a result of both chronic pain and
depression, in addition to other psychiatric illnesses that he has described.
He thought that she had lost confidence and said it is possible she will
improve psychologically once litigation is settled, but he commented that
individuals out of work for more than two years usually become demoralized and
have difficulty returning to work.

[
295
]

He thought that R.V.E. would benefit from psychological
intervention.  She needs specific treatment related to post-traumatic stress
disorder and the impact of the abuse upon her personality development and her
inter-personal relationships.  He said that given the chronicity and degree of
the impact he would think that she would require relatively long-term therapy
with a psychologist, which he estimated at about 30-40 sessions or longer at a
current rate of $140 per hour.  One of the problems, he said, is that patients
sometimes have an aggravation of distress.  The other problem with counselling
is that she has multiple other disorders – depression, chronic pain – and
whether she will benefit remains to be seen.

[
296
]

Therefore, in summary, I conclude that it has been proven on a
balance of probabilities that the cause of R.V.E.’s post-traumatic stress
disorder, anxiety disorder and personality problems was the plaintiff’s sexual
and physical abuse.  In terms of depression, I accept Dr. O’Shaughnessy’s
opinion that it is probable that the sexual abuse played a significant role,
causing the initial depression, but other factors, i.e. chronic pain from the
accidents and arthritis added to the severity of this mood disorder.  I also
accept his opinion that her alcohol abuse would not have occurred had the
sexual abuse not occurred.

[
297
]

I expect that when this litigation is completed that R.V.E.’s
symptoms will diminish somewhat and that her depression, substance abuse and
sexual dysfunction will remain in remission if properly treated by medication.
I expect however that she will continue to suffer chronic pain from the
injuries from the car accident and from the arthritis that she suffers from.

[

]

The defendant’s counsel submits that even if she cannot prove that

[

]

I will first discuss applicability of the defence of qualified
privilege in the circumstances.  Then I will discuss whether the plaintiffs
